newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: OLYMPICS-COMMERCIALISM, CULTURE COMBINE IN SAN JUAN.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-COMMERCIALISM, CULTURE COMBINE IN SAN JUAN.

text.p: San Juan, an outsider in the race to stage the 2004 Olympics, combines the exuberant commercialism of the United States with the rich culture of Latin America.

About 1,600 km southeast of Miami, the Puerto Rican capital offers an often harsh juxtaposition of the two cultures and is home to about one million of the Caribbean island's 3.8 million people. Another 2.7 million Puerto Ricans are estimated to reside on the U.S. mainland.

In the centuries-old walled city of Old San Juan, a branch of the Atlanta-based Hooters restaurant chain, known for waitresses in orange hot pants, sits just down the street from Fort San Cristobal, a stone fortress completed in 1772.

On another street, a modern supermarket lies a short distance from an arena used for cockfighting, a favourite sport of gamblers which is illegal in the United States but so popular that Puerto Rico has a government office to monitor it.
"It is an advantage that we are so close to the United States, the world's largest media market," Marimer Olazagasti, president of the 2004 commission, said.

While San Juan's air and water quality have been judged acceptable, sceptics think its size could be its greatest obstacle to winning the Summer Games, which have not been held in Latin America since the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City.

Puerto Rico has been a U.S. possession for 99 years, since Spain ceded it to the United States after the Spanish-American War. Its residents are U.S. citizens, although they do not vote in presidential elections or pay federal income taxes.
But Puerto Rico has retained the trappings of nationhood, including its own Olympic team. And it is as a developing city seeking Olympic status that San Juan organisers make their case for the games.

"We believe you can send a big message, a strong message to the world that Olympicism and the Olympics are not just for the big cities or the developed countries. That a small island, in progress, and trying to develop as fast as this society can, should have the oportunity to host the most extraordinary event in the world," Olazagasti said.
She noted that public opinion polls have shown 94 percent of Puerto Ricans support San Juan's Olympics bid.

The island has some clout with Olympic officials. Richard Carrion, president of Puerto Rico's Banco Popular, is chairman of the International Olympic Committee's Finance Committee, while the city. hosted the successful 1979 Pan American games.

Organisers said they can raise the $1.3 billion to pay for the games through television and radio rights, corporate sponsorships, ticket sales, and souvenir sales. They said 76 percent of the facilities needed are already in place, with four more under construction, and a city rail transport system that would boost transportation during the games is planned.

San Juan's biggest drawbacks include a shortage of hotel rooms, but Olazagasti said plans are in place to boost San Juan to more than 20,000 by 2004, versus its current 10,000 to 12,000. She also noted San Juan's giant cruise ship port could host ships serving as seaborne hotels.
